sub_criteria.name: default effect size
sub_criteria.text: Measures how much an opt-out, opt-in, or active-choice enrolment design changes participation or contribution rate, ideally with an effect size.

sub_criteria.name: persistence and depth
sub_criteria.text: Follows outcomes beyond initial sign-up: retention, withdrawal, disengagement, or amount actually saved at 6 months or more.

sub_criteria.name: anchoring on preset levels
sub_criteria.text: Addresses whether a pre-set contribution amount, multiplier, or slider default anchors the level people end up choosing.

sub_criteria.name: consumer self-directed setting
sub_criteria.text: Studies adults choosing for themselves in a consumer financial, fintech, or digital product, not an employer-mediated retirement plan.

sub_criteria.name: distributional and manipulation risk
sub_criteria.text: Reports heterogeneity in who benefits or is harmed, welfare effects, or when a default is perceived as manipulative or a dark pattern.

sub_criteria.name: active choice comparison
sub_criteria.text: Compares active/forced choice enrolment against opt-in or opt-out defaults on enrolment and engagement outcomes.

items.title: Beyond pink and blue: how gender roles mediate sex differences in risk-taking
items.abstract_600: Risk-taking propensity is a key factor behind decisions spanning economics, finance or health. Studies show males tend to take more risk than females, albeit reasons remain debated. The authors investigate this on a large student sample (n = 3,236), examining whether a gender measure (BEM-sex role inventory) mediates the relationship between biological sex and risk taking. items.abstract_600: Cognitive overload can impair professional skepticism in high‐stakes contexts such as auditing. In these settings, sustaining professional skepticism is essential. Default nudges, or pre‐selected options, may offset these effects by reducing cognitive demands. items.title: The effect of probability and framing on the default effect in decision making under risk
items.abstract_600: This study examines how probability and outcome framing modulate the default effect in risky decision-making using two controlled experiments with probabilistically equivalent lotteries. Participants repeatedly chose among four equivalent betting options, with one highlighted as a default. items.title: Resisting Humanization: Ethical Front-End Design Choices in AI for Sensitive Contexts
items.abstract_600: Ethical debates in AI have primarily focused on back-end issues such as data governance, model training, and algorithmic decision-making. items.title: A Systematic Review of User Experiments on the Effects of Dark Patterns
items.abstract_600: Deceptive/Manipulative Patterns (DMP) are interface designs, also known as “dark patterns,” that manipulate user behavior. While considerable attention has been paid to their ethical and legal implications, empirical evidence about their real-world effects remains diffuse. This review synthesizes up-to-date experimental studies, focusing on works that quantify how (or whether) DMPs influence users.
